Every candidate tells me he has spoken to our alumni. Very few can tell me what an alumnus actually said. So when I ask about it, I am checking two things. First, did you really have the conversation, or did you read the testimonials on our website? The testimonials are fine, but they are written to sell. A real conversation always contains something the website does not say, something that surprised you or even worried you. Second, what did you do with it? If an alumna told you that the learning team was the hardest part of the program, I want to know how you are preparing for that. The best candidates quote one person, by name, and then tell me what changed in their plan because of that conversation.

People ask me whether the program was worth the money, and my answer is always the same. The part that paid off was not the part I paid for. The classes were good, and some of the professors were excellent. But the thing that changed my career was a man who sat next to me in the first residency, a hospital director from Lisbon whose problems were almost exactly the same as mine. For eighteen months he was my sounding board, and I was his. We still speak every month. The certificate is in a drawer somewhere. If you are thinking about applying, my advice is simple. Choose the program where the people in the room are the ones you want to learn from, not the one with the best ranking.
